**My reasoning:**

I've been farming this same land in Quzhou my whole life. My father farmed it before me. Here, everyone grows wheat in winter and maize in summer — that's just what the land is for. The soil is flat, the wells are here, the buyers and the seed shops are set up for these two crops. I don't need to think hard about this.

My household has about 10 mu. My two children are in the city, so it's mostly me and my wife now. 10 mu is manageable for us.

For wheat, I'll use the Kenong 199 variety — the seed station sells it and my neighbor got good yields last year. I apply compound fertilizer at planting and top-dress with urea at jointing. I irrigate at the wintering stage, again at jointing, at heading, and at grain filling — four times is what I've always done, the wheat needs it here, we don't get enough rain. I'll spray herbicide in the spring flush, then fungicide for the mildew, and watch for aphids near heading — usually three spray runs.

For maize, I plant immediately after wheat harvest in June, no time to waste. I use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed, which I buy every year — my own saved seed never does as well. I use no-till planting directly into the wheat stubble, it saves time and the machine does it fast. Maize gets a lot of rain in July and August so usually I only need to pump once, maybe at tasseling if July is dry. I spray herbicide early and watch for corn borer.

I expect around 450 kg/mu for wheat and 550 kg/mu for maize. That's normal for here. Not great years, not bad years.

Wheat is planted in October using improved Kenong 199 variety with rotary tillage, heavy fertilizer application, and four groundwater irrigations to compensate for the dry North China Plain climate. Maize follows immediately after the June wheat harvest using hybrid Zhengdan 958, planted no-till to save time, relying mostly on summer rainfall with one supplemental irrigation.
